case_title: Vinod Jaswantray Vyas (Dead) Through Lrs v. The State of Gujarat
accused_victim_relationship: Police officer (accused) and arrested person (victim) in custody; the victim's sisters denied any prior relationship with the accused; the defence alleged a vengeance motive
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 read with s.114 (conviction altered by High Court to IPC s.304 Part I)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-1, PW-2, PW-3); medical (post-mortem and Medical Jurist PW-9, expert letter PW-10); documentary (telegram Exhibit-14, complaint Exhibit-13)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 r/w s.114 IPC; life imprisonment and fine of Rs. 25,000 each (default 2 years RI)
high_court_outcome: Appeal partly allowed; guilt affirmed but conviction altered from s.302 to s.304 Part I IPC; 8 years RI and compensation of Rs. 50,000 to heirs
neutral_facts: The victim, who had been arraigned as an accused in a criminal case registered at a police station, came to that police station late at night, accompanied by his advocate and two sisters, to surrender. The prosecution case is that two police officers, the accused, assaulted the victim with fists and sticks at separate intervals inside the police station, causing multiple injuries across his body, after which he became unconscious and was placed in a lockup. The next evening the victim was produced before a Magistrate, who remanded him to judicial custody, and he was lodged in a central prison, where his condition deteriorated. He was taken to a civil hospital and declared dead early the following morning. Two sisters testified that they saw the beatings, and a third detainee in the lockup also gave evidence. The sisters described blows landing on the back, arms, chest, thighs and ankles. A telegram sent by one sister to the state police headquarters alleged custodial torture, and a formal complaint followed about three weeks after the incident. The post-mortem examination recorded multiple external abrasions and bruises and internal injuries, including fractures of the sternum and ribs and ruptures of the lung, liver and spleen. The medical jurist opined that the injuries were fresh, occurring within six to eight hours of death, and that a person with such injuries could not climb stairs without support. An inquest witness described red dust on the clothing, and the jail soil was said to be red. The advocate was not examined as a witness.
physical_harm: Death of the victim; multiple external abrasions and bruises, fractures of sternum and ribs, and ruptures of lung, liver and spleen
number_of_offences: 2 charged (IPC s.302 and s.114, the latter as abetment); 0 finally upheld
motive: Not identified (the court found the motive theory attributed by the prosecution witnesses 'not palpable'; defence alleged vengeance by family)
key_evidence_accepted: Medical Jurist (PW-9) evidence and post-mortem report (Exhibit-50) on fresh injuries and inability to climb stairs; the court did not accept the eyewitness account as reliable
witness_credibility: Eyewitnesses PW-1 and PW-2 held not of sterling worth (unnatural conduct, contradicted by medical evidence); PW-3 found to suffer from grave infirmities, contradictions and omissions
bail_history: A1 granted bail, with sentence suspended by order dated 6 June 2017
trial_duration: offence: 10 June 1992; trial judgment: 4 March 1997; High Court: 13 February 2017; Supreme Court: 09 July 2024
legal_representation: Accused (appellants): Harin P. Raval, Sr. Adv., with Anando Mukherjee and others; State of Gujarat (respondent): Ms. Deepanwita Priyanka, with Ms. Swati Ghildiyal and Ms. Devyani Bhatt
investigation_status: Magisterial inquest held; complaint registered; cognizance taken under s.302 IPC; charges framed; trial completed with 10 prosecution witnesses
procedural_irregularity: Investigating agency did not make extensive inquiry from prison authorities; advocate, co-detainee Anna Dorai and wife not examined; expert letter (Exhibit-53) marked without proof of contents
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted, life imprisonment; High Court: conviction altered to s.304 Part I, 8 years RI; Supreme Court: acquitted
prosecution_argument: Concurrent findings should not be disturbed; sisters had no reason to falsely implicate; PW-3 gave clinching evidence; delay explained by fear of retribution and prompt telegram; police influence over investigation
defence_argument: Delay of about 20 days in complaint; no motive; only the victim was injured; injuries more probably caused in jail given fresh-injury opinion and red soil; eyewitnesses unnatural and a false case by family
legal_principle_applied: Unnatural conduct of eyewitnesses discredits testimony; where medical evidence completely demolishes ocular version, the ocular evidence may be disbelieved; mere marking of an exhibit does not prove its contents
precedent_relied_upon: Lahu Kamlakar Patil v. State of Maharashtra (2013) 6 SCC 417; Shivasharanappa v. State of Karnataka (2013) 5 SCC 705; Narendrasinh Keshubhai Zala v. State of Gujarat [2023] 2 SCR 746; Harvinder Singh v. State of Himachal Pradesh [2023] 13 SCR 1157; Chunthuram v. State of Chhattisgarh (2020) 10 SCC 733; Sait Tarajee Khimchand (1972) 4 SCC 562; Narbada Devi Gupta (2003) 8 SCC 745; Bhajan Singh v. State of Haryana (2011) 7 SCC 421
other_sentence_order: Trial court and High Court judgments quashed and set aside; benefit of acquittal extended to co-accused A2 though no appeal was preferred on his behalf; pending applications disposed of
